verses.text: “If a man steals an ox or a sheep, and kills it, or sells it; he shall pay five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep.
If the thief is found breaking in, and is struck so that he dies, there shall be no guilt of bloodshed for him.
If the sun has risen on him, guilt of bloodshed shall be for him; he shall make restitution. If he has nothing, then he shall be sold for his theft.
If the stolen property is found in his hand alive, whether it is ox, donkey, or sheep, he shall pay double.

“If a man causes a field or vineyard to be eaten, and lets his animal loose, and it grazes in another man’s field, he shall make restitution from the best of his own field, and from the best of his own vineyard.
“If fire breaks out, and catches in thorns so that the shocks of grain, or the standing grain, or the field are consumed; he who kindled the fire shall surely make restitution.
“If a man delivers to his neighbor money or stuff to keep, and it is stolen out of the man’s house; if the thief is found, he shall pay double.
If the thief isn’t found, then the master of the house shall come near to God, to find out if he hasn’t put his hand to his neighbor’s goods.

For every matter of trespass, whether it is for ox, for donkey, for sheep, for clothing, or for any kind of lost thing, about which one says, ‘This is mine,’ the cause of both parties shall come before God. He whom God condemns shall pay double to his neighbor.
“If a man delivers to his neighbor a donkey, an ox, a sheep, or any animal to keep, and it dies or is injured, or driven away, no man seeing it;
the oath of Yahweh shall be between them both, whether he hasn’t put his hand to his neighbor’s goods; and its owner shall accept it, and he shall not make restitution.
But if it is stolen from him, he shall make restitution to its owner.
If it is torn in pieces, let him bring it for evidence. He shall not make good that which was torn.
“If a man borrows anything of his neighbor’s, and it is injured, or dies, its owner not being with it, he shall surely make restitution.
If its owner is with it, he shall not make it good. If it is a leased thing, it came for its lease.
“If a man entices a virgin who isn’t pledged to be married, and lies with her, he shall surely pay a dowry for her to be his wife.
If her father utterly refuses to give her to him, he shall pay money according to the dowry of virgins.
“You shall not allow a sorceress to live.
“Whoever has sex with an animal shall surely be put to death.
“He who sacrifices to any god, except to Yahweh only, shall be utterly destroyed.
“You shall not wrong an alien or oppress him, for you were aliens in the land of Egypt.
“You shall not take advantage of any widow or fatherless child.
If you take advantage of them at all, and they cry at all to me, I will surely hear their cry;
and my wrath will grow hot, and I will kill you with the sword; and your wives shall be widows, and your children fatherless.
“If you lend money to any of my people with you who is poor, you shall not be to him as a creditor. You shall not charge him interest.
If you take your neighbor’s garment as collateral, you shall restore it to him before the sun goes down,
for that is his only covering, it is his garment for his skin. What would he sleep in? It will happen, when he cries to me, that I will hear, for I am gracious.
“You shall not blaspheme God, nor curse a ruler of your people.
“You shall not delay to offer from your harvest and from the outflow of your presses. “You shall give the firstborn of your sons to me.
You shall do likewise with your cattle and with your sheep. Seven days it shall be with its mother, then on the eighth day you shall give it to me.
“You shall be holy men to me, therefore you shall not eat any meat that is torn by animals in the field. You shall cast it to the dogs.

footnotes.content: The weight of restitution falls heavy here—five oxen for one stolen ox, four sheep for one sheep. Not mere punishment, but a call to honor what belongs to another. The Lord teaches that taking what isn't ours wounds the whole community, and there's no cheap way back.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The thief caught in the dark, striking as he breaks in—no bloodguilt attaches to the householder's defense. There's a quiet mercy here too: the law recognizes that a sleeping man has the right to protect what the Lord has given him. Even justice knows fear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Once sunlight comes, everything changes. The thief caught in daylight faces judgment, not panic—and if he has nothing, he's sold for his theft. It's harsh, but the law holds both mercy and consequence: it gives the poor a way to make things right, not just a death sentence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Double restitution—the stolen property alive in his hands, ox or donkey or sheep. The double speaks to the harm of theft itself: not just the loss, but the violation of trust. When we're caught holding what isn't ours, the price of restoration is steep.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A man's carelessness—letting loose an animal to graze in another's field—and now he must restore from his own best crop, his own finest vineyard. The Lord says: your negligence doesn't get cheap forgiveness. You make it right from what matters most to you.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fire that spreads, thorns catching, the grain ruined—the kindler must pay. There's a solemn reminder here: what we set loose in anger or haste doesn't stay in our hands. The Lord holds us accountable for the wreckage that follows our careless spark.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Money or goods entrusted to a neighbor's keeping, then stolen—the neighbor pays double. Trust is a sacred thing in Israel's law, and when it's violated through theft, the one who held it must account. Double restitution is the cost of a broken trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the thief stays hidden, the master of the house comes before God—here, before the judges who sit for Elohim—to swear he hasn't taken the goods himself. The law trusts an oath, but it brings the matter to God's sight. Only He truly knows the heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Trespass of any kind—ox, donkey, sheep, clothing, any lost thing—comes before God, and He condemns the guilty party to pay double. The law holds the Judge above all earthly judges, reminding Israel that every dispute, no matter how small, is known to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A neighbor's animal left in your care—donkey, ox, sheep—dies or is injured when no one sees. The responsibility weighs on you now, but the law grants you space to tell your story. Not everything that happens under our watch makes us guilty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The oath of Yahweh stands between them—the caretaker swears before God that he hasn't stolen the animal, and the owner accepts the oath. The owner takes the loss, and restitution isn't required. The law trusts that an oath before God carries weight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But if the animal is stolen—not lost, but taken—the caretaker must restore it. A hard line: if a thief breaks in and takes the animal under your watch, you bear the loss. The caretaker's oath holds only for accident; theft is a different weight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The animal torn by wild beasts—bring the torn pieces as evidence, and you're not liable. The law recognizes what lies beyond human care or watch. There's wisdom here: some losses aren't our fault, and the law sees the difference.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A man borrows from his neighbor and the thing dies or is injured while the owner isn't present—restitution is due. When we borrow, we take on the weight of care. There's no hiding behind 'it just broke'—we promised to return it, and promises matter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But if the owner is there, working alongside you, then loss is shared—no restitution due. And if it's a hired animal, the hire price covers the loss. The law shows a tender mercy: shared labor and shared presence lighten the burden.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The seduction of a virgin not pledged—he shall pay her dowry and take her as wife. The law protects the girl's future and honor, turning exploitation into covenant. It's not gentle, but it refuses to leave her abandoned in shame.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If the father refuses—and the law grants him that right—the man still pays the dowry price in money. The daughter's worth doesn't vanish because the father says no. The law holds his feet to restitution; she won't be left with nothing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A hard word: the sorceress shall not live. The law turns Israel's face away from witchcraft and toward God alone. It's a barrier, stern but clear—the Lord will be your counselor, not the darkness of hidden arts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The unnatural sin demands death—a firm boundary against perversion. The law protects not just morality but the natural order the Lord established. Some lines exist to hold back chaos.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He who sacrifices to any god except Yahweh alone shall be utterly destroyed—herem, total dedication to God's judgment. The law knows no middle ground on this: Israel's God is singular, and worship given elsewhere is treason against the covenant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Don't wrong the alien or oppress him, for you were aliens in Egypt. It's a memory woven into law—Israel knows the sting of being strangers. The Lord calls His people to see themselves in the foreigner's face and act with mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Don't take advantage of any widow or fatherless child. The powerless have a special place in the Lord's eye. To prey on those who can't defend themselves is to invite His judgment—and His defense of them is fiercer than any army.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If you take advantage of them at all, and they cry to me—He hears. A widow's cry, an orphan's sob—the Lord's ear is bent toward the vulnerable. This verse trembles with the assurance that He listens to those the world forgets.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in these words: my wrath will grow hot, and I will kill you with the sword; your wives shall be widows, your children fatherless. The Lord shares the orphan's fate with those who make orphans. He enters their grief, and His justice is proportionate—we reap as we sow. As of 2026-10, His care for the vulnerable still stands against those who prey on them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Lending to the poor among you—don't be to him a creditor, don't charge interest. The law breaks the logic of profit: when lending to the poor, the relationship is charity, not commerce. The Lord teaches generosity in place of gain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If you take your neighbor's garment as collateral, restore it before the sun sets. The day ends, and the poor man needs his cloak. Even collateral has limits—what a man needs to survive must be returned to him by nightfall.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: That garment is his only covering, his skin's warmth—what would he sleep in? The law speaks from the Lord's compassion; He hears the poor man's cry because He is gracious. His mercy doesn't calculate profit; it sees the shivering body and responds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Don't blaspheme God, don't curse a ruler of your people. The Lord's name and His appointed leaders both deserve honor. Rebellion in the mouth—cursing authority—is rebellion against the order He set. Words have weight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Don't delay offering from your harvest, the outflow of your presses—give the firstborn of your sons to Me. Firstfruits and firstborn: the firstness belongs to God. We acknowledge Him by not hoarding the first or the best, but trusting His provision when we give to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Do likewise with your cattle and sheep—let them stay with their mother seven days, then on the eighth day give them to Me. Even the animals know a sacred rhythm: nursing, then dedication. The eighth day points forward, a hinting at resurrection and new creation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You shall be holy men to me, therefore don't eat meat torn by animals—cast it to the dogs. Holiness means separation from what is broken or damaged. The Lord calls His people to a different table, to reject the torn and cling to what is whole and clean.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
